segments.title: Trading older capital ships for new construction
segments.summary: The counterfactual begins by asking what the Royal Navy might receive if it surrendered more 13.5-inch ships, including HMS Tiger, under the Washington settlement.
segments.body: Britain receives extra construction tonnage only by surrendering older ships. The possible 525,000- and 558,950-ton totals permit five or six 35,000-ton replacements while reducing the number of hulls available for overseas stations. Giving up HMS Tiger also removes one of the Royal Navy's four fast capital ships, so the new class has to restore that operational capability. The treaty bargain therefore ties design choices to fleet presence and availability.

evidence.note: The transcript sets out exchanging 13.5-inch ships for five or six new ships under alternative tonnage totals.

segments.title: Why a capability needs more than one hull
segments.summary: Several fast capital ships give the Royal Navy dependable availability across maintenance and deployment cycles.
segments.body: One ship provides a capability only when available, while two provide it in normal circumstances but leave no depth for a casualty or refit. Three allow continuous availability, and larger numbers add presence and surge capacity. Surrendering Tiger makes this rule especially important because the treaty bargain reduces the fast force as well as the battle line. Fleet value therefore depends on the ships that can actually deploy after accounting for maintenance, damage, and other commitments.

evidence.note: The speaker lays out the progression from one available capability to continuous availability and surge capacity.

segments.title: Why fewer British hulls might unlock treaty consent
segments.summary: The alternative treaty deal becomes diplomatically plausible because Britain would exchange nine older ships for only five or six new ones, reducing how many places its capital ships could cover.
segments.body: The proposed bargain improves British ship quality while cutting the number of British hulls that American or Japanese planners might face. That loss of geographic presence gives the United States and Japan a reason to consider the arrangement even though the replacement ships would be more capable. Either navy might still demand permission to complete another 16-inch-gun ship of its own. Under that arithmetic, five ships at the 525,000-ton ceiling are the cautious outcome.

evidence.note: The transcript weighs the reduced British hull count against possible American and Japanese demands, then returns to the 525,000-ton limit.

segments.title: A 28-knot alternative to Nelson and Rodney
segments.summary: The proposed alternative is a 35,000-ton capital ship with 16-inch guns and 28-knot speed, using less protection than the historical two-ship Nelson design.
segments.body: The design begins with the loss of HMS Tiger and the need to retain a fast element in the fleet. A 28-knot ship offers a G3-influenced compromise between a conventional battleship and a battlecruiser. The game model stays within eight tons of Nelson and Rodney's stated full-load displacement while rearranging the main turrets and placing three triple 6-inch secondary turrets aft. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts imposes practical limits on the reconstruction. The result is a visual experiment in what modestly reduced protection might buy when Britain can procure several ships instead of two.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes 35,000 tons, 16-inch guns, and 28 knots, then introduces the simulated design.

segments.title: Quantity versus armour in the battle line
segments.summary: More 28-knot ships could make a powerful fast battle line even if each vessel accepted less armour than Nelson and Rodney.
segments.body: With only two ships, armour takes priority because each loss is strategically severe. With four, five, or six, a common 28-knot class becomes more attractive than an exceptionally protected pair. Modernized Queen Elizabeth-class ships could then join the same fast battle line, making speed and numbers mutually reinforcing. The slower R-class would retain secondary duties but become the obvious next group for replacement.

evidence.note: The speaker contrasts armour for a two-ship force with a 28-knot class of four to six ships.

segments.title: Why a small speed margin can cost operational radius
segments.summary: A nominally faster enemy may have to run continuously at maximum speed to stay clear of a 28-knot British battle line, sharply reducing its useful radius.
segments.body: The comparison distinguishes top speed from the speed a fleet can sustain economically across an operation. A 30-knot opponent has only a narrow margin over ten British ships capable of 28 knots. Keeping that margin may require sustained maximum-power steaming instead of normal cruising speed. The resulting fuel and endurance penalty turns a two-knot paper advantage into a strategic constraint on where the faster ship can operate or escape.

evidence.note: The speaker explains that a 30-knot ship must use maximum speed to remain beyond a 28-knot battle line, shortening its operational radius.

segments.title: Testing the design against Bismarck
segments.summary: A simulated Denmark Strait-style action illustrates how two 16-inch ships can overwhelm a faster opponent despite lighter protection.
segments.body: The game scenario is not offered as a historical prediction, but as a way to visualize the design trade. The hypothetical ships retain a substantial belt while yielding some protection for speed and a more numerous force. Two ships bring eighteen 16-inch guns against Bismarck's eight 15-inch guns, making concentration of firepower the point of the demonstration. The engagement also shows the difficulty of escaping a fast battle line when sustained high speed reduces operational radius.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses reduced armour, the simulated Bismarck opponent, and the effect of double the number of heavy guns.

segments.title: Weight savings in the secondary battery and conning tower
segments.summary: The game design stays within its displacement target by reducing conning-tower protection, using three triple 6-inch turrets, and considering single mounts to represent 4.7-inch anti-aircraft guns.
segments.body: The simulated design reaches its weight target partly by cutting conning-tower protection, an acknowledged expedient of the model. Three triple 6-inch turrets halve the number of secondary mountings while providing nine secondary guns. The saved weight raises the possibility of adding single 5-inch game mounts to stand in for 4.7-inch anti-aircraft guns. Protection, secondary-armament layout, and anti-aircraft fit all compete for the same treaty-limited displacement.

evidence.note: The transcript admits reducing conning-tower protection, notes that triple 6-inch mounts halve the turret count, and considers single game mounts representing 4.7-inch anti-aircraft guns.

segments.title: Procurement is about a fleet, not one ship
segments.summary: Naval procurement distributes capability across a fleet, balancing heavily protected ships against the resilience that comes from larger numbers.
segments.body: Nelson and Rodney are formidable anchors of a battle line, but a pair must be treated as irreplaceable assets. The politicians would accept only two ships even though the Royal Navy wanted more. A larger class can accept a different balance between protection, performance, and loss tolerance. Procurement therefore starts with the capability the fleet must generate and works backward to platform size and count. The comparison extends to contemporary forces: larger, more expensive platforms may carry more capability, while smaller platforms provide presence in more places.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts two heavily protected ships with a larger class and explains fleet-level procurement choices.

segments.title: Penny packets versus complete force packages
segments.summary: A modern analogy contrasts small detachments suited to counterinsurgency with battle groups that need armour, artillery, and larger transport platforms against a proficient opponent.
segments.body: The discussion shifts from battleships to the modern problem of matching a deployed force to the opposition it may face. Small marine detachments can cover many places and may suffice against a local insurgency, but a stronger enemy demands a complete battle group with armour, artillery, and supporting capabilities. Larger ships can carry that heavier package, although their cost means buying fewer hulls and maintaining presence in fewer locations. The analogy makes the Nelson question concrete: platform size, force quality, geographic coverage, and budget must be balanced together.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts counterinsurgency detachments with larger combined-arms battle groups and relates platform size to presence.

segments.title: The machinery route to 28 knots
segments.summary: Reduced armour and a rearranged machinery plant are presented as the technical route from Nelson and Rodney’s 45,000 shp to a faster design.
segments.body: The original ships used two shafts, 45,000 shaft horsepower, eight boilers, and two geared turbines. The alternative has twelve three-drum boilers, three geared turbines, and three shafts while keeping one funnel. Induced draught and the third shaft save weight against the Royal Navy's usual four-shaft preference. This machinery sketch belongs to a hypothetical new class and carries the compromises expected from a game model. It explains why 28 knots becomes plausible once Britain is ordering several ships.

evidence.note: The speaker compares the historical machinery with a three-shaft, higher-power hypothetical arrangement.

segments.title: How a larger order could sustain industry
segments.summary: Building six Nelson-type ships in the 1920s would keep shipyards, armour manufacture, and their supply chains more active.
segments.body: The discussion identifies a second-order effect often hidden by a ship-to-ship comparison: capital-ship orders sustain industrial skills and capacity. Six ships would keep yards, armour manufacturers, and a broad supplier network employed through the 1920s. Depression-era pressures would still exist, but treaty-authorized construction could prevent these orders from being cancelled. The argument links fleet policy to the industrial base required to support later naval power.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies shipyards, armour production, and supply chains as effects of a six-ship programme.

segments.title: Why a stopped target becomes easier to hit
segments.summary: The simulated Bismarck's loss of motion illustrates why visual fire-control solutions become much simpler once a target stops manoeuvring.
segments.body: The game action pauses on the geometry behind the rapidly worsening result. Naval fire-control systems were designed to hit one moving ship from another moving ship using visual observations and estimates of relative motion. Once Bismarck is barely moving, much of that target-motion problem disappears and the British ships can maintain a steadier solution. The simulation simplifies real combat, but the moment illustrates why mobility and steering damage can be tactically decisive before a ship sinks.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts moving-target visual fire control with the much easier problem of firing at an almost stationary opponent.

segments.title: How turret layout changes the forward firing arc
segments.summary: The alternative main-battery arrangement can bring all nine 16-inch guns forward, unlike the protection-driven historical Nelson layout.
segments.body: As the British ships cross Bismarck's track, the game exposes an operational consequence of turret placement. The hypothetical design can bring its full main battery onto a forward target, while the historical Nelson arrangement restricts the aftermost turret in that arc. The historical arrangement concentrates protection and saves weight on a uniquely valuable pair. Armour concentration, turret geometry, and tactical firing arcs have to be considered together.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Bismarck's restricted fire, the historical Nelson arrangement, and the hypothetical design's ability to fire all main guns forward.

segments.title: A fast battle line would reshape rival designs
segments.summary: A Royal Navy battle line of 28-knot ships would force Germany and the United States to reconsider the speed, displacement, and protection of their own capital ships.
segments.body: A 30-knot German battleship may no longer have enough margin to evade a large British force that can sustain 28 knots. The resulting pressure would affect decisions about machinery, armour, displacement, and operational roles. American planners would also face a British line substantially faster than their standard battleships. British carriers would need to operate with the faster battle line as well.

evidence.note: The transcript connects a 28-knot Royal Navy line to German, American, and carrier-design consequences.

segments.title: Five ships as the conservative treaty outcome
segments.summary: Five 35,000-ton ships are presented as the cautious estimate, enough to form a fast line alongside modernized Queen Elizabeth-class battleships.
segments.body: The treaty arithmetic makes five ships the more conservative result. The historical Nelsons displaced about 33,800 tons standard, leaving roughly 1,200 tons within the 35,000-ton unit assumed for the alternative class. Combined with five Queen Elizabeths modernized to 28 knots, five Revenge-class ships, and the battlecruisers, this would produce eighteen British capital ships. Ten of the battleships could form a common 28-knot line while Renown, Repulse, and Hood remain a still-faster squadron. The later 28-knot King George V design supports this speed as a plausible British benchmark. The older Revenge class would receive less modernization attention and become the next replacement priority.

evidence.note: The speaker identifies five ships as conservative and describes the resulting 28-knot British battle line.

segments.title: Why a two-ship pair produces a different design
segments.summary: Nelson and Rodney's unusual priorities suit a unique two-ship capability. A standardized class of five or six would begin from different requirements.
segments.body: The counterfactual exercise explains British capital-ship design practice. A pair built for one scarce role has to be treated differently from a standardized class of five or six ships. The larger class can accept less individual protection in exchange for common speed, wider availability, and greater loss tolerance. The size of the order therefore changes the design requirement before engineers begin choosing armour, machinery, or layout.

evidence.note: The transcript explicitly contrasts British design practice for a two-ship pair with the requirements of a larger class.

segments.title: Why the Revenge class becomes the slow secondary line
segments.summary: Retiring the 13.5-inch battleships leaves the Revenge class as the fleet's only 21-knot group and clarifies why it would become the next replacement priority.
segments.body: The counterfactual changes the meaning of ships that remain as well as the ships Britain builds. Once the older 13.5-inch battleships disappear, the Revenge class becomes the only 21-knot component of a fleet increasingly organized around faster units. The class was a cheaper secondary line that retained the Queen Elizabeth class's 15-inch battery while giving up speed and therefore cost. That earlier procurement logic now makes the ships a useful reserve but also the obvious obstacle to a common 28-knot battle line and the next candidates for replacement.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the Revenge class as the remaining 21-knot group and explains its cheaper, slower relationship to the Queen Elizabeth class.

segments.title: Modernizing the Queen Elizabeth class for a common speed
segments.summary: A 28-knot Nelson class would give the Royal Navy a stronger reason to modernize the Queen Elizabeth class to match its battle-line speed.
segments.body: The Warspite reconstruction shows that additional boilers and altered internal arrangements could support higher speed. Subdivided boiler rooms and another pair of boilers could extend that work toward 28 knots. Historically, the fleet did not have the same incentive because the R-class and the two slower Nelsons set a different tempo. In this scenario, a common 28-knot speed makes modernization of the Queen Elizabeths a fleet-level priority.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Warspite's boiler arrangements to argue that Queen Elizabeths could be raised to 28 knots.

segments.title: Why treaty-maximum guns made the pair precious
segments.summary: As Britain's only treaty-maximum 16-inch-gun battleships, Nelson and Rodney had to emphasize survivability over the speed that a larger class could exploit.
segments.body: The counterfactual helps explain the priorities of the ships Britain actually built. Nelson and Rodney would be the fleet's only 16-inch-gun battleships, carrying the maximum calibre permitted by the Washington treaty and considerable status as a result. Because there were only two costly hulls, losing either would remove half of this capability, making protection and survivability more valuable than pushing for 28 knots. A two-ship fast squadron would also be small enough for rival navies to design around, whereas five or six common-speed ships could reshape the whole balance of the battle line. Their unusual armour and layout follow from that fleet policy and the risks of concentrating the capability in two hulls.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the pair as Britain's sole treaty-maximum 16-inch battleships and explains why survivability outweighs speed for only two hulls.

segments.title: Deployment options for a faster British battle line
segments.summary: A larger fast capital-ship force opens different choices for Mediterranean, Far Eastern, and Atlantic deployment.
segments.body: With five or six ships, the Nelson squadron need not remain concentrated at home as a uniquely scarce asset. The discussion suggests a Mediterranean role, Queen Elizabeths as reinforcement for the Far East, and R-class ships in the Atlantic as later reinforcements. Renown, Repulse, and Hood would retain the mobile diplomatic and Atlantic duties of the battlecruiser squadron. Numbers and common speed create strategic flexibility before a battle is ever fought.

evidence.note: The transcript sketches Mediterranean, Far East, and Atlantic roles for the alternative battle squadrons.
